subtopic_detail: Persistent sense of watching himself from outside four months after stopping heavy cannabis use
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 23 year old apprentice who stopped daily cannabis four months ago after a frightening episode of palpitations and breathlessness while smoking. Since that night he has felt, in his words, like he is watching himself in a film and operating his own body by remote control.

Colours look flat to him and familiar rooms seem staged, as though nothing is quite solid. He knows none of this is actually true and finds that reassuring and maddening at the same time. He has had no voices, no beliefs that others are controlling him and no sense that thoughts are being put into his head. He has started refusing shifts on the customer counter because he is afraid someone will see that something is wrong with him.

data_table.Examination: Anxious, fully oriented, no thought disorder, no perceptual abnormality elicited, neurological examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, thyroid stimulating hormone 1.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start risperidone 1 mg at night and review his perceptual symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: An antipsychotic would be indicated if reality testing were lost, and it is not: he knows the experience is subjective and internally generated, which is precisely what separates this from a psychotic perceptual disturbance. Antipsychotics have no established benefit here and several reports describe worsening of the detachment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and an electroencephalogram
options.rationale: Structural and electrical investigation is warranted when detachment is episodic and stereotyped with automatisms or postictal confusion, suggesting temporal lobe seizures. His symptoms are continuous, have a clear precipitant and come with a normal neurological examination, so the yield is close to zero. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Start propranolol 20 mg twice daily and review his perceptual symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Beta blockade dampens the autonomic component of panic and would have helped on the night the symptoms began, but it does nothing for the sustained detachment that followed. Treating the physical symptoms of anxiety alone leaves the avoidance that now drives his impairment untouched. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Reassure him that the symptoms are a withdrawal effect and review him in six months
options.rationale: Cannabis withdrawal peaks in the first week and has largely resolved by four weeks, so symptoms still present at four months are no longer withdrawal. Six months of watchful waiting also allows the avoidance to consolidate at the point where it is still easily reversed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy targeting symptom monitoring and avoidance
options.rationale: Persistent detachment from the self and from surroundings with intact reality testing, following a panic episode and cannabis use, responds best to psychoeducation plus cognitive behavioural therapy that reduces symptom monitoring, catastrophic appraisal and safety behaviours. Naming the experience as a recognised and non-psychotic phenomenon is itself therapeutic because most patients fear they are becoming psychotic. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

explanation.summary: Depersonalisation and derealisation are among the commonest psychiatric symptoms in the general population and are usually transient, but as a persistent disorder they are chronically under-recognised and are often mistaken for an emerging psychosis. Intact reality testing is the defining feature: the patient knows the experience is a distortion of their own perception rather than a change in the world. Cannabis, ketamine, panic attacks and sleep deprivation are the usual precipitants, and the symptom then self perpetuates as the patient scans for it and interprets it catastrophically. Treatment is psychoeducation and cognitive behavioural therapy aimed at reducing that monitoring and the associated avoidance, with a serotonin reuptake inhibitor added only for comorbid depression or anxiety rather than for the detachment itself. Average delay to correct diagnosis is measured in years, largely because patients struggle to describe the experience and fear they will be thought mad if they try.
key_points: Intact reality testing separates this from a psychotic perceptual disturbance
Cannabis, ketamine, panic and sleep deprivation are the common precipitants
Symptom monitoring and catastrophic appraisal maintain the disorder
Cognitive behavioural therapy with psychoeducation is first line
Antipsychotics are unhelpful and may worsen the detachment
explanation.pearls: Cannabis withdrawal symptoms peak at two to six days and are essentially gone by four weeks, so any perceptual or mood symptom still present beyond a month after cessation should be reclassified as a primary disorder rather than attributed to withdrawal and watched.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: Short day sleep and racing thoughts four weeks into a run of night shifts in an emergency nurse
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34 year old emergency department nurse who is four weeks into a block of night shifts. She sleeps about four hours during the day, lies awake feeling wired at four in the morning on shift, snaps at her partner, and has been buying things online at three in the morning that she does not need.

She says her thoughts feel fast and jumbled, but when asked she describes herself as worn out rather than energised and says what she wants most is more sleep. There is no history of elevated mood, no grandiosity, no increase in goal directed activity and no reduction in her perceived need for sleep. On her five days off at the end of the previous block she slept eight hours a night and everything settled within two days. Her bedroom faces east and has thin curtains, and her neighbour is renovating.

data_table.Examination: Tired in appearance, normal rate and rhythm of speech, affect reactive, no flight of ideas, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.0 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start lithium and arrange a serum concentration measurement after five days
options.rationale: A mood stabiliser assumes a bipolar diagnosis, and the cardinal feature of hypomania is a reduced need for sleep with preserved or increased energy, whereas she is exhausted and wants more sleep. Committing a patient to lithium on shift related symptoms carries lifelong monitoring and renal and thyroid consequences. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Start quetiapine 100 mg before her day sleep and review her mood in two weeks
options.rationale: Sedating antipsychotics are sometimes used off label as hypnotics, but the metabolic and next day sedation burden is unacceptable in someone who drives home after a night shift, and it treats the symptom rather than the circadian misalignment causing it. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Advise a fixed sleep schedule with timed light exposure and a dark bedroom
options.rationale: Insomnia and impaired alertness tied to a shift schedule, resolving within two days of returning to a normal routine, is a circadian rhythm problem rather than a mood disorder, and the treatment is behavioural: an anchored sleep period, bright light during the first part of the shift, dark glasses on the drive home and a blacked out quiet bedroom. Fixing the light and noise exposure addresses both the short day sleep and the irritability that follows it. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift work and sleep)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift work and sleep

options.text: Start temazepam 10 mg before her day sleep and review her sleep in two weeks
options.rationale: A hypnotic may lengthen day sleep a little but does not realign the circadian clock, and tolerance plus residual sedation are real risks in a worker whose job involves drug calculations and who then drives. It is reserved for short term use after the behavioural measures have been put in place. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Refer urgently to the mental health service for assessment of elevated mood
options.rationale: Urgent referral would be right if there were sustained elevated or irritable mood with reduced need for sleep persisting away from the trigger, and the crucial history here is that everything remitted within forty eight hours on her days off. Impulsive overnight spending during sleep deprivation is not by itself evidence of hypomania. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Shift work disorder is insomnia or excessive sleepiness occurring in relation to a work schedule that overlaps the usual sleep period, and it affects roughly a fifth to a third of rotating and night shift workers. It mimics hypomania closely because sleep deprivation produces irritability, racing thoughts, impulsive spending and emotional lability, and it mimics depression because of the fatigue and withdrawal that follow. The discriminator is the relationship to the roster: circadian symptoms track the schedule and remit within a few days of returning to normal sleep, while a genuine mood episode persists independently. Management is behavioural and environmental first, with an anchored sleep period, bright light early in the shift, light avoidance on the journey home, a blacked out and quiet bedroom, and strategic napping before the shift. Melatonin taken before the day sleep and short term hypnotics are second line, and modafinil is reserved for persisting sleepiness under specialist supervision.
key_points: Reduced need for sleep with high energy defines hypomania; wanting more sleep argues against it
Remission within days of returning to a normal roster points to a circadian cause
Anchored sleep, timed bright light and a dark quiet bedroom are first line
Sedating antipsychotics and hypnotics do not realign the circadian clock
Sleep deprivation alone can produce irritability, fast thoughts and impulsive spending
explanation.pearls: Wearing dark glasses on the drive home after a night shift is one of the highest yield single interventions available, because morning daylight on the retina is the strongest signal shifting the circadian clock in the wrong direction, and blocking it typically lengthens subsequent day sleep by around an hour.

sources.label: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift work and sleep
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Blocked hallways and inability to discard possessions after a fire service safety notice
stem:
You are the general practitioner visiting a 71 year old widow at home after the fire service attended a smoke complaint and issued a safety notice. Newspapers, containers and clothing are stacked chest high through the house, with a single narrow path between rooms, the kitchen bench and stove are not usable, and she sleeps in an armchair.

She agrees that the fire risk is real and says she is ashamed of the state of the house, but becomes visibly distressed when you pick up an empty ice cream container, explaining that she may need it. She has no beliefs that the items are alive or contaminated and no voices. Her daughter cleared the lounge room two years ago while she was in hospital; the room refilled within four months and they did not speak for a year afterwards. She manages her own banking and medications without error.

data_table.Examination: Well kempt and well nourished, no squalor and no animals, Mini-Mental State Examination 28 out of 30, no delusions elicited, distress on handling of possessions
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.6 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), vitamin B12 420 pmol/L (150-700), full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange a forced clean out with the council and review her at home in three months
options.rationale: Forced clearance reliably produces rapid re-accumulation and severe distress, and her own history demonstrates exactly that pattern with the loss of the relationship that went with it. It is reserved for imminent danger that cannot be managed any other way, and even then it is done alongside treatment rather than instead of it. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Refer for hoarding specific cognitive behavioural therapy with a case manager
options.rationale: Difficulty discarding driven by a perceived need to save, with accumulation that renders living areas unusable, responds to a disorder specific cognitive behavioural approach targeting decision making, beliefs about possessions and graded sorting practice, coordinated with housing and fire safety services. Working with her rather than around her is what prevents the re-accumulation that followed the previous clearance. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Start fluvoxamine 100 mg daily and review her living conditions in three months
options.rationale: Serotonin reuptake inhibitors help the obsessive compulsive disorder that sometimes sits alongside this condition, but response rates for the saving and difficulty discarding themselves are modest and lower than for obsessive compulsive disorder proper. Medication is an adjunct, not the initial plan. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Arrange neuropsychological testing and brain imaging to look for cognitive decline
options.rationale: New accumulation with self neglect in an older person does warrant a cognitive assessment, and frontal syndromes can present this way, but she scores 28 out of 30, manages her banking and medications accurately and retains full insight into the risk. The behaviour here is driven by distress on discarding rather than by an inability to organise. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Apply for a guardianship order to allow decisions about her accommodation
options.rationale: Substitute decision making requires impaired decision making capacity, and she understands the risk, retains information and manages complex tasks independently, so the threshold is not met. Poor judgement in the eyes of others is not the same as absent capacity. (Source: Australian Guardianship and Administration Council)
source_refs: Australian Guardianship and Administration Council

explanation.summary: Hoarding disorder became a diagnosis in its own right in 2013 and is defined by persistent difficulty discarding possessions because of a perceived need to save them, with distress on discarding and accumulation that compromises the use of living areas. Prevalence rises steeply with age and reaches several per cent in people over 70, and the main risks are fire, falls, structural collapse, infestation and eviction. Insight varies, and its presence does not predict ability to act, which is why exhortation and clearance both fail. Effective treatment is a structured cognitive behavioural programme adapted for this disorder, delivered over many months and often in the home, combined with practical coordination between the general practitioner, housing, council, fire services and family. Comorbid depression, anxiety and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder are common and worth screening for because they impede engagement.
key_points: Difficulty discarding due to a perceived need to save, with unusable living areas, defines it
Forced clearance produces rapid re-accumulation and ruptured relationships
Disorder specific cognitive behavioural therapy with multi-agency coordination is first line
Serotonin reuptake inhibitors are adjunctive with modest effect on the hoarding itself
Capacity is preserved in most cases, so guardianship is rarely appropriate
explanation.pearls: Fire is the lethal risk to quantify for the family: hoarded dwellings account for a disproportionate share of fatal residential fires because the fuel load blocks egress and defeats firefighter entry, which is why a working smoke alarm and a cleared exit path are negotiated at the first visit, ahead of any sorting work.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: Aerosol propellant inhalation in a fifteen year old with a rash around the mouth and falling grades
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 15 year old boy brought in by his mother, who found a dozen empty deodorant cans under his bed. Over three months his grades have dropped from good to failing and he has stopped going to football.

She describes him coming home some afternoons unsteady on his feet with slurred speech that clears within about an hour, and she has noticed a chemical smell on his clothes. He is guarded but eventually says he does it with two friends behind the shops because it is free and quick. There are no injection marks and no tremor. He denies alcohol and cannabis and his breath alcohol reading today is zero.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Erythematous cracked skin around the mouth and nostrils, conjunctival injection, no needle marks, gait normal today, no cerebellar signs
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), alanine aminotransferase 28 units/L (5-35), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start naltrexone 50 mg daily and refer him to a youth drug and alcohol service
options.rationale: Naltrexone blocks opioid receptors and has a role in alcohol and opioid use disorders, neither of which is in play here, and there is no pharmacotherapy with established efficacy for volatile substance use. Prescribing it also implies a mechanism that does not apply. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Arrange an urgent blood lead concentration and start chelation if the level is raised
options.rationale: Lead toxicity is the specific concern with leaded petrol sniffing, which produces encephalopathy, tremor and ataxia, and chelation is then genuinely indicated. Aerosol propellants are butane and related hydrocarbons and contain no lead, so the test does not fit the substance described. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology

options.text: Start nicotine replacement and refer him to a youth drug and alcohol service
options.rationale: Nicotine replacement treats nicotine dependence, and nothing in the history points to smoking or vaping as the problem to solve. Offering it risks the adolescent concluding that the clinician has not understood what he disclosed. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Notify child protection services and arrange an involuntary admission today
options.rationale: Statutory notification is required where there is a reasonable belief of abuse or neglect, and an engaged parent seeking help is the opposite of that picture; involuntary admission requires a mental illness meeting the criteria of the mental health legislation, which volatile substance use alone does not satisfy. Both responses tend to end the therapeutic relationship at the moment it is most useful. (Source: National Health and Medical Research Council: Volatile substance use guidance)
source_refs: National Health and Medical Research Council: Volatile substance use guidance

options.text: Refer him to a youth drug and alcohol service and involve his parents in the plan
options.rationale: There is no effective pharmacotherapy for this pattern of use, so management is psychosocial: engagement with a youth specific service, family involvement, attention to the school disengagement that both causes and results from the use, and harm reduction advice about the cardiac risk. Treating the peer and school context is what shifts the behaviour. (Source: National Health and Medical Research Council: Volatile substance use guidance)
source_refs: National Health and Medical Research Council: Volatile substance use guidance

explanation.summary: Volatile substance use is concentrated in early adolescence because the products are cheap, legal and everywhere, and it is under-detected because standard urine drug screens do not include hydrocarbons, so a negative screen never excludes it. The examination clue is the rash around the mouth and nose from repeated contact with propellant, along with a chemical odour on clothing and short lived intoxication that clears within an hour. Chronic use causes cognitive impairment, cerebellar damage, renal tubular acidosis with toluene, and bone marrow suppression with benzene containing products. The acute killer is sudden sniffing death, in which myocardial sensitisation to catecholamines produces ventricular fibrillation during a surge of adrenaline, classically when the user is startled or chased. Management is entirely psychosocial: a youth specific alcohol and other drug service, family engagement, re-engagement with school and harm reduction advice, because no medication has been shown to help.
key_points: Standard urine drug screens do not detect hydrocarbons, so a negative result excludes nothing
Rash around the mouth and nose with a chemical odour is the physical sign
Intoxication is brief, typically resolving within an hour of last use
No pharmacotherapy is effective; management is psychosocial and family based
Toluene causes renal tubular acidosis and chronic use causes cerebellar damage
explanation.pearls: Advise the family never to chase or startle him while he is intoxicated: sudden sniffing death occurs when a catecholamine surge triggers ventricular fibrillation in a myocardium sensitised by the hydrocarbon, and it can occur on a first exposure, which is why the safest response to finding him mid-use is a calm approach rather than confrontation.

sources.label: National Health and Medical Research Council: Volatile substance use guidance

subtopic_detail: Night time fall at home in a 70 year old taking temazepam every night for eight years
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 70 year old woman who fell getting up to the toilet two nights ago. She grazed her elbow, there was no fracture and she did not lose consciousness.

She has taken temazepam 20 mg every night for eight years, started during the months after her husband died, and she also takes amlodipine. She tells you the tablet does not really work any more but that she lies awake for hours if she misses it, and she has come in today mainly to make sure the script does not run out. She lives alone, still drives during the day and does her own shopping. She remembers the fall clearly and describes feeling groggy and slow on her feet rather than dizzy or faint.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: No postural drop on lying and standing measurement, normal gait and tandem walk, no cerebellar or peripheral neurological signs, visual acuity corrected to 6/9 bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram sinus rhythm with normal intervals, vitamin B12 380 pmol/L (150-700), creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her medication?

options.text: Switch her to zopiclone at an equivalent dose and review her sleep in four weeks
options.rationale: The so called non-benzodiazepine hypnotics act at the same receptor complex and carry the same falls, fracture and motor vehicle crash risk in older people, so this swaps the label rather than the hazard. It also resets tolerance expectations and restarts the dependence clock. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

options.text: Stop the temazepam now and start melatonin, reviewing her sleep in four weeks
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after eight years of nightly use risks rebound insomnia, severe anxiety and, occasionally, withdrawal seizures, and it guarantees she will resume the tablet. Prolonged release melatonin is a reasonable adjunct in this age group but not a substitute for a planned taper. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Continue the current dose and reassess her falls risk again in twelve months
options.rationale: Continuing is the path of least resistance and is what usually happens, but the fall has already occurred, she describes grogginess rather than presyncope, and the postural blood pressure and cardiac assessment are normal, so the sedative is the modifiable contributor sitting in front of you. A year is far too long given the fracture risk. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

options.text: Reduce the temazepam by a quarter of the dose every two weeks with sleep advice
options.rationale: A gradual reduction negotiated with the patient, paired with behavioural sleep measures, is the approach that achieves lasting cessation in long term users, and a step of about a quarter of the dose every one to two weeks is tolerable while allowing slowing near the end. Her normal cardiac and postural findings make the sedative the target worth changing. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

options.text: Convert her to diazepam and reduce that gradually over the next three months
options.rationale: Conversion to a long half-life agent is a recognised technique for short acting benzodiazepines, but it is specifically cautioned against in older people and in hepatic impairment because diazepam and its active metabolites accumulate and worsen the very sedation and falls risk being treated. The difference from the correct answer is not the taper but the drug it is run on. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

explanation.summary: Long term nightly benzodiazepine use in older adults produces tolerance to the hypnotic effect within weeks while the impairment of balance, reaction time and memory persists indefinitely, which is why patients commonly report that the tablet no longer works but that they cannot stop. The associated harms are falls and hip fracture, motor vehicle crashes and accelerated cognitive impairment, and the risk is dose related but present at low doses. Deprescribing succeeds when it is negotiated rather than imposed, tapered gradually over weeks to months, and supported by behavioural treatment for the insomnia underneath, since the original sleep problem usually remains. Rates of success in general practice rise substantially when the conversation is framed around the falls or the memory rather than around dependence. Withdrawal seizures are rare but real after abrupt cessation of high dose or very long term use, which is the safety reason a taper is not optional.
key_points: Tolerance to the hypnotic effect develops but the balance and memory impairment does not
Gradual dose reduction of about a quarter every one to two weeks is well tolerated
Substituting a non-benzodiazepine hypnotic carries the same risk profile
Diazepam conversion is cautioned against in older people because of accumulation
Behavioural treatment of the underlying insomnia must run alongside the taper
explanation.pearls: Frame the taper around driving and hip fracture rather than dependence: benzodiazepine use in older adults roughly doubles the risk of a motor vehicle crash and of hip fracture, and the fracture risk is highest in the first two weeks after a dose increase or a new prescription, which is also the argument against switching her to another hypnotic.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice
